title: Why wouldn’t Manchester United renew Harry Maguire’s contract?
content:
Manchester United will do the right thing by renewing Harry Maguire’s contract. Yes, the defender turned 33 this month, but it makes sense on several levels. He’s still a top-quality centre-back performing consistently for the club. Replacing him could cost tens of millions — money United need to prioritise on signings elsewhere in the team.

His form has been so impressive that he’s been recalled by England for their March internationals having not been involved since September 2024, and he should add to his 64 caps in this week’s games against Uruguay and Japan. His dream of playing in the 2026 World Cup come June and July is not over.

Maguire is well respected in the United dressing room. Likeable, mature and settled, he connects well with staff and is seen as a positive influence on his peers.

He had suitors who wanted to sign him in the recent winter window or at the end of this season, when his current contract runs out. In January, a fee would have been required. Given he wasn’t playing for them at the time, United would have given any offer the consideration it deserved. But everyone wanted to get Maguire as a free agent in the summer.

Four clubs from Italy’s Serie A showed concrete interest, along with three Premier League sides and one of Turkish football’s giants. And why not when you’d be getting a top player for no fee – which would’ve meant more money for Maguire than his present wage, which he is likely to stay on in any new deal, at United.

Despite knowing the interest, United didn’t rush into negotiating with Maguire. Why should they? Nor did his camp know of the club’s intentions. Good. There was an example in recent years where a United manager was very honest with a player — which is how he liked to be — and told him, with six months of the season remaining, that his contract would not be getting extended. That player’s performances then dipped significantly for the remainder of the season and his time at Old Trafford.

With Maguire, he was best off showing his worth on the pitch and negotiating from there.

Unlike on previous occasions, Maguire didn’t rush back to play when he was 90 per cent fit. He’s learned from doing this in the past and won’t take to the pitch when carrying niggles again. He waited until he was 100 per cent and, at the start of the year, he was ready to return. That coincided with Michael Carrick’s first game after succeeding the sacked Ruben Amorim at home to Manchester City and — like his friend and ex-United team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer — the interim coach has a very high opinion of Maguire. This has been vindicated as he has started every game so far under the former United midfielder, helping to deliver seven wins, two draws and only one defeat.

Carrick also returned to a back four, which Maguire much prefers, though he’ll miss the next game against Leeds United after being sent off against Bournemouth last Friday.

His next appearance will be his 600th in senior club football, following spells at Sheffield United (166), Hull City (75), Wigan Athletic (16 on loan) and Leicester City (76) before his summer 2019 move to Manchester (266).

And then there’s Maguire the footballer, the defender who is also a goal threat in the opposition penalty area. Yes, there are limitations to his game, which we’ll come to, but they are vastly outweighed by the positives.

“You have to look at Harry in a glass-half-full way in order to understand what he brings to the team, and that’s how the coaches look at him,” explains one source who has worked closely with Maguire at United, speaking anonymously to protect relationships.

“Every single manager or head coach he’s had at United has ended up using him consistently in the team because he brings leadership, calm, and composure. He brings physical strength and is a magnet to the ball, especially defensively when we’re defending the box. Some centre-backs will only worry about their man, because they don’t have a burning desire to go and win the ball, but Harry does. He sees it as a responsibility: he’s the biggest guy, the strongest, the best aerially. Coaches love that.

“Sometimes it can be late in the game when teams are going more direct. He shields the ball extremely well, and because he’s so big and strong, once he puts his leg in front of you, it’s very hard to get the ball off him. He can use that momentum to start an attack as well.”

It’s not completely true that every single United manager he’s had has started him all the time. Erik ten Hag didn’t, and neither did Amorim. It was notable that while Maguire sent a social-media message of goodwill to every other departed United manager or head coach he’d worked under when they left, Ten Hag was the exception.

He also lost the captaincy under the Dutchman and started only eight of the 38 league games in his 2022-23 debut season as manager, but Ten Hag began to start him again because he (belatedly) recognised the qualities that others see.

“His threat in the opposition box, his strength and power, is a massive asset,” says the same source. “He’s very good at beating blockers on attacking set plays and players who aren’t as big as him but who get deployed against him. He powers through them, he’s brave and aggressive in the opposition box, he has good timing.”

But it’s not all about using his size.

“On the ball, his calmness and composure mean opponents don’t feel confident pressing him because they know he has the quality with both feet to play through and around blocks. But when you do press him, he has ball security and protection, so that can cause you problems.”

Maguire averaged 41 appearances per season in his first six years at Old Trafford, but won’t play that many in this one because United can only have a maximum of 40 matches due to failing to qualify for Europe and going out of both domestic cups early. He’s also had a thigh injury, which kept him out for nine league fixtures from the end of November.

Given his age, he’s unlikely to be playing every time should United return to a 50-games-plus schedule next term, but, unlike this season, when he started on the bench with Matthijs de Ligt and Leny Yoro preferred ahead of him, while Luke Shaw played on the left of Amorim’s 3-5-2, he looks like a cert on the team sheet again.

Yoro and Ayden Heaven are young defenders at the club who Maguire rates extremely highly, but they’re aged 20 and 19 respectively and need time to improve and find the consistency he already has. Those two can learn with him (or the injury-afflicted De Ligt and Lisandro Martinez) alongside them on the pitch. He can help them in many ways, not least when it comes to dealing with the pressure of being a United player, and he deserves credit for the manner in which he overcame online abuse from some of the club’s own fans around 2022.

Maguire’s rehabilitation in the minds of even the most critical among the United support is complete, but his game is not.

“One legitimate complaint is that he sometimes takes so long on the ball that he slows down attacks — opponents can be 100 per cent organised,” the source quoted above says. “In Ruben’s rigid formation, it allowed the opponents to be confident in their positioning because there isn’t a lot of movement. If you are slow at the back as a unit, opponents can defend as they want.

“In certain types of game, Harry could have possibly done better to vary the ball more and change his positioning to provoke the opposition or create different angles.”

We can critique, but if Maguire signs a one-year extension as expected (and United’s style is to add another year option on top of that, so the club can decide whether to renew in 12 months’ time), it will be welcomed by the club, by the player, and by most United fans in a turnaround of opinion which is in most part due to his character and dignified determination to face down the critics via his actions on the field.
